⚠️ The Missing WHERE Clause Disaster
Omitting the WHERE clause in an UPDATE or DELETE statement will apply the change to every single row in your entire table. If you miss this, you risk permanently overwriting or erasing your entire database instead of modifying one specific record.
⚠️ The Identity Column Insertion Error
When a table uses an Identity or auto-increment column for the Primary Key, you must omit that column from your INSERT column list. If you try to manually provide a value for an auto-incrementing ID, the database will throw an error and block the insertion.
⚠️ The Unstable Primary Key Trap
Using a person's name or email address as a Primary Key is considered bad practice because these values are not guaranteed to be unique or permanent. If a user changes their email address, you break the relational links across your entire database, which is why using a dedicated ID number is essential.
⚠️ The SELECT * Performance Bottleneck
Using the * wildcard to retrieve all columns is inefficient for large databases and should be avoided in production code. If you use it unnecessarily, you waste system memory and network bandwidth by pulling data that your application doesn't actually need.
